title: No-code fine-tuning: Mark Hennings
talk_summary: Mark Hennings pitches no-code fine-tuning as a way to replace long engineered prompts with a smaller fine-tuned model trained on about 20 structured examples, then evaluate against the prompt baseline and improve from production logs. The demo is mostly vendor UI, but the copyable workflow is prompt prototype -> structured dataset -> fine-tune -> eval -> deploy -> log feedback.

takeaways.technique: Fine-tune narrow high-volume tasks to shrink prompts and use cheaper models
takeaways.what_they_do: They collect input/output examples for a specialized task, fine-tune a lighter model, and keep only the unique input plus a short system prompt at inference.
takeaways.evidence_quote: fine tuning is awesome it's faster and cheaper because you can train a lighter model to match the quality of what you were doing with a prompt
takeaways.numbers: GPT-4 196 ms/token vs GPT-3.5 73 ms/token (3x faster); 88.6% cheaper; prompts 90% shorter in one example

takeaways.technique: Eval fine-tune against prompt-engineered baseline before routing
takeaways.what_they_do: They explicitly compare the fine-tuned model to the prompt-engineered version and test which models reach the same performance level.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we should evaluate it to make sure that it actually is better than the prompt engineered version

takeaways.technique: Hybrid system prompt plus fine-tuned behavior
takeaways.what_they_do: They keep a short system prompt for instructions while the fine-tune learns repetitive style/rubric behavior from examples.
takeaways.evidence_quote: which creates this really interesting hybrid between prompt engineering and fine tuning

takeaways.what_they_do: They log real production examples and user feedback, then add them back to the training/eval dataset for continuous improvement.
takeaways.evidence_quote: from production we can capture feedback from our users and we can log the examples

takeaways.technique: Structured example datasets instead of monolithic prompts
takeaways.what_they_do: They store training examples as structured fields/templates so a team can edit and extend them like code, rather than one giant prompt.
takeaways.evidence_quote: training data is this layer that your team can work on and add to and edit and improve
